newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt sees U.S. plan addressing unilateral moves.
newsitem.headline: Egypt sees U.S. plan addressing unilateral moves.

text.p: A U.S. initiative in the Middle East is likely to require Israel to refrain from unilateral steps on Jerusalem and other "final status" questions, a senior adviser to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Thursday.
Adviser Osama el-Baz, also a senior foreign ministry official, told Reuters Television in an interview that without such an element any U.S. initiative would be doomed anyway.

Such a requirement is likely to meet stiff Israeli resistance. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who will meet U.S. President Bill Clinton next week, vowed on Thursday not to relinquish a right to settle Jews on occupied land.

"(The Americans) are thinking of ways and means to convince the Israeli prime minister to refrain from taking any unilateral actions, whether they relate to Jerusalem, the settlements or other issues that are supposed to be settled in the final status negotiations," Baz said.

"We don't know what the package will be, what it will look like at the end. We know that they are thinking in terms of three issues -- stopping violence, on the other hand refraining from any unilateral action by Israel and, third, preparing right away for the resumption of the talks," he added.

Asked how he rated the chances of success, Baz said a good test would be whether the Israelis froze building work on their settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa, the East Jersualem site that has brought the peace process to an impasse.

"If they are willing to do so, even in a de facto manner, the process can be revived and the American initiative can succeed. Otherwise I'm afraid to say that the American initiative can go down the drain," he said.
"Unnecessarily we'll be wasting not only our time and effort but also the time and effort of the superpower that has the prime responsibility for advancing peace," he added.
Baz said U.S. policy in the Middle East appeared confused because of the conflicting pressures on the U.S. administration.
"We sense that they are not happy with the exercise of their veto power in the Security Council twice because they think it has given the Israeli cabinet the wrong signal," he said.
The United States vetoed two resolutions critical of the Jabal Abu Ghneim settlement on the grounds that the Security Council was not the appropriate forum for discussing it.
"On the other hand they don't want to be forced into a head-on collision with the Israeli government, they don't want to get into conflict with the (Jewish) lobby," Baz said.
The adviser said that if peace talks collapsed, advocates of violence would carry the day and win more influence.
"This will open the door to outside intervention by extremist elements and so on, Iran and others -- this would be the nightmare scenario," he added.
